title: When rest feels like something you have to earn
author: Shayla Martinez-O'Brien, LPC
excerpt: A draft. If you can only rest once the list is finished, you will never rest, because the list is not a finite object.
heroAlt: Evergreens in the foreground with a mountain peak catching the last warm light of the day.
body: This one is still a draft — it's here so you can see what an unpublished post looks like in the editor.

A lot of people I see are not, by their own account, struggling. They're functioning. They get up, they do the work, they show up for the people who need them. What they'll say, if you give it long enough, is that it costs more than it used to.

Somewhere along the way rest became conditional. You can sit down once the kitchen is clean, once the emails are answered, once the week is under control. The logic feels responsible. The problem is that the list is not a finite object — it regenerates faster than you clear it — so the condition is never met, and the rest never comes.
## What usually has to change first
Not the schedule. The belief underneath it, which is generally some version of: my worth is what I produce.
That belief tends to have a history. Often it was true once, in a household or a job where slowing down genuinely wasn't safe. It made sense then. It just kept running after the conditions changed.
Pick one small block of rest and put it before the work rather than after. Fifteen minutes. Deliberately unearned.
Most people find this uncomfortable, which is the useful part. The discomfort is the belief objecting, and that's the thing we can actually work with.
